From the compact SVD to the least-norm solution, and from weight decay to data augmentation: the tools that make learning stable and robust

21.1 The Compact SVD and Pseudo-Inverse Definition

In Lecture 10 we introduced a quick-and-dirty pseudo-inverse: $(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$. It works beautifully when $X^TX$ is invertible, but fails the moment $X$ is rank-deficient or has more columns than rows. The singular value decomposition gives us a far more principled tool — one that is defined for every matrix, agrees with the ordinary inverse whenever an inverse exists, and has elegant geometric and algebraic properties that make it the right object for understanding least-squares regression in full generality.

Before defining the pseudo-inverse we revisit the two flavors of SVD introduced in the previous lecture, because the choice between them is not merely cosmetic — it is what makes the pseudo-inverse cleanly invertible in its middle factor.

21.1.1 Recap of the Compact SVD

Any matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ of rank $r$ admits two related decompositions. The full SVD pads the middle diagonal matrix out to $n \times d$ with zeros, filling in extra orthonormal columns in $U$ and $V$. The compact SVD keeps only the $r$ nonzero singular values and discards everything else. It is the compact form that we need here.

Definition · Compact SVD

Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ have rank $r$. The compact (thin) SVD of $X$ is the factorization $$X = U \Delta V^T$$ where $U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$ has orthonormal columns ($U^TU = I_r$), $\Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}$ is diagonal with strictly positive diagonal entries $\delta_1 \ge \delta_2 \ge \cdots \ge \delta_r > 0$ (the singular values), and $V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ has orthonormal columns ($V^TV = I_r$). The columns of $U$ are the left singular vectors; the columns of $V$ are the right singular vectors.

The key distinction from the full SVD is that $\Delta$ is square and invertible. There are no zero diagonal entries because we keep only the $r$ positive singular values. This invertibility is the property that unlocks the pseudo-inverse.

💡
Why compact? The compact SVD discards directions in which $X$ has no "signal" (zero singular values). Those directions contribute nothing to $X$ and nothing to $X^+$; keeping them would only complicate the algebra. The compact SVD is the minimal sufficient representation of $X$.

21.1.2 Defining the Moore-Penrose Pseudo-Inverse

With the compact SVD in hand the definition is strikingly simple: just reverse the order of the factors and invert the middle matrix — exactly what you would do for an ordinary inverse if $X$ were square and invertible.

Definition · Moore-Penrose Pseudo-Inverse

Let $X = U \Delta V^T$ be the compact SVD of $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$. The Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of $X$ is $$X^+ = V \Delta^{-1} U^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}.$$ The diagonal entries of $\Delta^{-1}$ are $1/\delta_1, 1/\delta_2, \ldots, 1/\delta_r$ — the reciprocals of the nonzero singular values of $X$. Zero singular values are not inverted; they are simply absent from the compact SVD.

Notice that $X^+$ has dimensions $d \times n$ — exactly the dimensions of $X^T$. This is not a coincidence. As we will see in Section 21.3, $X^+$ and $X^T$ share the same singular vectors; they differ only in their singular values. The pseudo-inverse replaces each singular value $\delta_i$ with its reciprocal $1/\delta_i$, while the transpose leaves them unchanged.

Example · Computing a Pseudo-Inverse

Setup. Let $X = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}$. The rank is $r = 2$.

Step 1 — Find the SVD. By inspection (columns are already orthogonal): the left singular vectors are $u_1 = e_1 = (1,0,0)^T$, $u_2 = e_3 = (0,0,1)^T$; the right singular vectors are $v_1 = e_1 = (1,0)^T$, $v_2 = e_2 = (0,1)^T$; and the singular values are $\delta_1 = 3$, $\delta_2 = 2$. So $U = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\Delta = \begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, $V = I_2$.

Step 2 — Invert. $X^+ = V \Delta^{-1} U^T = I_2 \cdot \begin{pmatrix}1/3&0\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1/3&0&0\\0&0&1/2\end{pmatrix}.$

Verification. $XX^+ = \begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1/3&0&0\\0&0&1/2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix} = UU^T$. The middle row and column are zero because the second standard basis vector $e_2 = (0,1,0)^T$ is in the left null space of $X$ — it lies outside the column space.

21.2 Fundamental Identities of the Pseudo-Inverse

The four identities in this section are the algebraic backbone of the pseudo-inverse. They tell us what $XX^+$ and $X^+X$ look like, and they pin down exactly when the pseudo-inverse acts as a genuine left or right inverse.

21.2.1 Products $XX^+$ and $X^+X$

Theorem · Products of $X$ and $X^+$

Let $X = U\Delta V^T$ be the compact SVD. Then:

  1. $XX^+ = UU^T$  (symmetric, $n \times n$)
  2. $X^+X = VV^T$  (symmetric, $d \times d$)
Proof

Part 1. Substituting the definitions: $$XX^+ = (U\Delta V^T)(V\Delta^{-1}U^T).$$ Since $V^TV = I_r$ (compact SVD property), the $V^TV$ in the middle collapses: $$XX^+ = U\Delta (V^TV) \Delta^{-1}U^T = U\Delta I_r \Delta^{-1}U^T = U(\Delta\Delta^{-1})U^T = UU^T.$$ Symmetry: $(UU^T)^T = (U^T)^TU^T = UU^T$. $\checkmark$

Part 2. By the identical calculation with roles of $U$ and $V$ swapped: $$X^+X = (V\Delta^{-1}U^T)(U\Delta V^T) = V\Delta^{-1}(U^TU)\Delta V^T = V\Delta^{-1}\Delta V^T = VV^T. \quad \checkmark$$ □

Intuition · What $UU^T$ and $VV^T$ Do

$UU^T$ is the orthogonal projector onto the column space of $U$, which equals the column space of $X$. It maps any vector $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ to its closest point in Col($X$). Similarly, $VV^T$ projects onto the row space of $X$. So multiplying $X$ by $X^+$ does not give the identity — it gives the identity on the column space and zero elsewhere. This is the best a non-square, rank-deficient matrix can do in lieu of a true inverse.

21.2.2 Right and Left Inverses When Rank Is Maximal

Theorem · Right and Left Inverses

Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ with compact SVD $U\Delta V^T$ and rank $r$.

  1. If $r = n$ (full row rank), then $XX^+ = I_n$ and $X^+$ is a right inverse of $X$.
  2. If $r = d$ (full column rank), then $X^+X = I_d$ and $X^+$ is a left inverse of $X$.
  3. If $r = n = d$ (square and invertible), then $X^+ = X^{-1}$.
Proof

Part 1. If $r = n$ then $U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is square. From the compact SVD, $U^TU = I_n$. For a square matrix, $U^TU = I$ implies $UU^T = I$ (the transpose of a square orthogonal matrix is also its inverse). Therefore $XX^+ = UU^T = I_n$.

Part 2. Symmetric argument: if $r = d$ then $V$ is $d \times d$ square with $V^TV = I_d$, so $VV^T = I_d$ and $X^+X = VV^T = I_d$.

Part 3. If $r = n = d$ then both conditions hold simultaneously, so $X^+X = XX^+ = I$, meaning $X^+ = X^{-1}$. □

Part 3 is the sanity check for the entire theory: if the ordinary inverse exists, the pseudo-inverse reduces to it. There is no conflict between the two notions. For matrices that lack an inverse — singular square matrices, wide matrices, tall matrices — the pseudo-inverse is the natural generalization that recovers as much of the inverse's behavior as the rank allows.

Data Science Application · Design Matrices in Regression

In supervised learning the design matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ plays the central role. When $n > d$ and $X$ has full column rank ($r = d$), the system $Xw = y$ is overdetermined and the pseudo-inverse provides the unique least-squares solution $w^+ = X^+y = (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$. When $n < d$ (more features than samples), the system is underdetermined, $r < d$, and $X^+X \ne I_d$ — there are infinitely many solutions. The pseudo-inverse selects the minimum-norm solution among them (see Section 21.5). When features are correlated, $r < \min(n,d)$ and neither identity holds; only the full Moore-Penrose theory handles this correctly.

21.3 Compact SVDs of Related Matrices

One of the most illuminating aspects of the pseudo-inverse is how it relates to the transpose and how all three matrices — $X$, $X^T$, and $X^+$ — fit into a single coherent algebraic family. The key insight is that all three are compact SVDs in disguise, sharing the same singular vectors but differing in their singular values.

21.3.1 SVDs of $X^T$, $X^+$, and $(X^+)^T$

Theorem · Compact SVDs of Transpose and Pseudo-Inverse

Given the compact SVD $X = U\Delta V^T$, the following are compact SVDs:

  1. $X^T = V \Delta U^T$  —  same singular values, $U$ and $V$ swap roles
  2. $X^+ = V \Delta^{-1} U^T$  —  singular values inverted
  3. $(X^+)^T = U \Delta^{-1} V^T$  —  singular values inverted, $U$ and $V$ swap roles
Proof

Each factorization has the form $A = P \Sigma Q^T$ where $P$ and $Q$ have orthonormal columns and $\Sigma$ is diagonal with positive entries, so each is a compact SVD by definition. For (1): $(U\Delta V^T)^T = V\Delta^T U^T = V\Delta U^T$ (since $\Delta$ is diagonal, $\Delta^T = \Delta$). The orthonormality conditions $V^TV = I_r$ and $U^TU = I_r$ carry over directly. For (2): $X^+ = V\Delta^{-1}U^T$ by definition; $\Delta^{-1}$ is diagonal with positive entries $1/\delta_i$. For (3): $(X^+)^T = (V\Delta^{-1}U^T)^T = U(\Delta^{-1})^TU^T$... wait, $(V\Delta^{-1}U^T)^T = U\Delta^{-1}V^T$ since $(\Delta^{-1})^T = \Delta^{-1}$. □

The theorem reveals a beautiful symmetry: $X^+$ is to $X$ what $X^T$ is to $X$ — except the singular values are inverted. The singular vectors are identical. This means the pseudo-inverse "undoes" the stretching that $X$ applies in each singular direction, while $X^T$ keeps the same stretching. In terms of geometry, $X^+$ is the operation that reverses the bijection $X$ establishes between row space and column space (see Section 21.4).

Figure 21.4. Singular value spectra for an example matrix $X$ with five singular values. Blue bars show the singular values of $X$; red bars show those of $X^T$ (identical to $X$); green bars show those of $X^+$ (reciprocals $1/\delta_i$). Key takeaway: $X^T$ and $X$ share exactly the same spectrum, while $X^+$ inverts every singular value. Large singular values of $X$ become small in $X^+$, and vice versa — with dramatic consequences for numerical stability when any $\delta_i$ is close to zero.

21.3.2 Null Spaces and Four Fundamental Subspaces

The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix — column space, row space, null space, and left null space — are completely determined by its compact SVD. Comparing the SVDs of $X$ and $X^+$ immediately tells us how their subspaces relate.

Theorem · Null Spaces of $X$ and $X^+$

For $X = U\Delta V^T$:

  1. $\text{Null}(X) = \text{Null}(V^T)$ (the null space of $X$ equals the null space of its right factor)
  2. $\text{Null}(X^+) = \text{Null}(U^T)$ (the null space of $X^+$ equals the left null space of $X$)
  3. The four fundamental subspaces of $X^+$ are exactly those of $X$ with row space and column space swapped.
Proof

Part 1. $(\Leftarrow)$ Suppose $V^Tw = 0$. Then $Xw = U\Delta V^Tw = U\Delta \cdot 0 = 0$, so $w \in \text{Null}(X)$.

$(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $Xw = U\Delta V^Tw = 0$. Premultiply by $\Delta^{-1}U^T$: $\Delta^{-1}U^TU\Delta V^Tw = 0$. Since $U^TU = I_r$ and $\Delta^{-1}\Delta = I_r$, we get $V^Tw = 0$. Both implications hold, so $\text{Null}(X) = \text{Null}(V^T)$.

Part 2. The same proof applied to $X^+ = V\Delta^{-1}U^T$ (with $U$ playing the role of $V$) gives $\text{Null}(X^+) = \text{Null}(U^T)$. Since $\text{Null}(U^T) = \text{Null}(X^T)$ by the same argument applied to $X^T = V\Delta U^T$, we have $\text{Null}(X^+) = \text{Null}(X^T)$.

Part 3. Taking orthogonal complements (using Rank-Nullity: null space $\perp$ row space): $\text{Row}(X^+) = \text{Null}(X^+)^\perp = \text{Null}(X^T)^\perp = \text{Col}(X)$. Similarly $\text{Col}(X^+) = \text{Row}(X)$. □

SubspaceFor $X$For $X^+$
Column spaceCol($U$) = Col($X$)Col($V$) = Row($X$)
Row spaceCol($V$) = Row($X$)Col($U$) = Col($X$)
Null spaceNull($V^T$)Null($U^T$) = Null($X^T$)
Left null spaceNull($U^T$) = Null($X^T$)Null($V^T$) = Null($X$)

The table makes the symmetry manifest: $X^+$ has exactly the same four fundamental subspaces as $X^T$. In fact, $X^+$ and $X^T$ are equivalent from the perspective of subspace geometry — they differ only in how they scale vectors within those subspaces.

21.4 Geometric Interpretation: Projection and Bijection

The algebra of the previous sections becomes vivid when translated into geometry. The key picture is this: $X$ restricted to its row space is a bijection onto its column space. The pseudo-inverse $X^+$ restricted to the column space is the inverse bijection. When vectors wander outside these subspaces, both $X$ and $X^+$ project them back in before acting.

21.4.1 $XX^+$ and $X^+X$ as Orthogonal Projectors

Theorem · Projector Properties

$XX^+$ is the orthogonal projector onto Col($X$), and $X^+X$ is the orthogonal projector onto Row($X$). Specifically:

  1. $(XX^+)^2 = XX^+$ and $(X^+X)^2 = X^+X$  (idempotent)
  2. $(XX^+)^T = XX^+$ and $(X^+X)^T = X^+X$  (symmetric $\Rightarrow$ orthogonal)
  3. $XX^+y = y$ for all $y \in \text{Col}(X)$, and $XX^+y = 0$ for all $y \in \text{Null}(X^T)$
Proof

From Theorem 21.2, $XX^+ = UU^T$. We verify the three properties directly.

(1) $(UU^T)^2 = UU^TUU^T = U(U^TU)U^T = UI_rU^T = UU^T$. $\checkmark$

(2) $(UU^T)^T = (U^T)^TU^T = UU^T$. $\checkmark$

(3) Any $y \in \text{Col}(X) = \text{Col}(U)$ can be written $y = Uc$ for some $c \in \mathbb{R}^r$. Then $UU^Ty = UU^TUc = U(U^TU)c = Uc = y$. For $y \in \text{Null}(X^T) = \text{Null}(U^T)$: $UU^Ty = U(U^Ty) = U \cdot 0 = 0$. $\checkmark$  □

Figure 21.3. Geometric illustration of the projector properties in 2D. Left: $XX^+$ projects every input point (navy dots) orthogonally onto Col($X$) (red line), yielding the projection points (red dots). The dashed gold arrows show the orthogonal projection step. Right: $X^+X$ projects onto Row($X$) (blue line). Points already on the subspace map to themselves (eigenvalue 1); points off it are mapped orthogonally onto it (eigenvalue 0). Key insight: these projectors have only eigenvalues 0 and 1, with exactly $r$ eigenvalues equal to 1.

21.4.2 The Row-Space to Column-Space Bijection

The most conceptually satisfying way to understand the pseudo-inverse is as the inverse of a restricted function. Define $f: \text{Row}(X) \to \text{Col}(X)$ by $f(p) = Xp$. This map is well-defined because $X$ maps every vector in its row space to a vector in its column space. It is injective because distinct points in Row($X$) map to distinct points in Col($X$) — the only kernel of $X$ restricted to Row($X$) is $\{0\}$. And it is surjective by definition of column space. So $f$ is a bijection.

Core Result
$$X^+ \text{ is the inverse of } f: \text{Row}(X) \to \text{Col}(X), \quad p \mapsto Xp$$ $$\text{i.e.,} \quad f^{-1}(q) = X^+q \text{ for all } q \in \text{Col}(X)$$

The singular vectors make this bijection concrete. The right singular vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_r$ form an orthonormal basis for Row($X$), and the left singular vectors $u_1, \ldots, u_r$ form an orthonormal basis for Col($X$). The map $f$ sends each basis vector $v_i$ to $\delta_i u_i$ — it stretches by the singular value. The inverse $f^{-1}$ sends each $u_i$ back to $(1/\delta_i) v_i$ — it compresses by the reciprocal.

Figure 21.1. The pseudo-inverse as a bijection. The blue parallelogram represents Row($X$) and the gold parallelogram represents Col($X$), both embedded in their respective ambient spaces. The navy arrows labeled $X$ map from row space to column space; the green arrows labeled $X^+$ reverse the journey. The right singular vectors $v_1, v_2$ (blue/purple) form an orthonormal basis for Row($X$); the left singular vectors $u_1, u_2$ (red/teal) form an orthonormal basis for Col($X$). Vectors outside the named subspaces (gray, in the null spaces) are projected to zero by $X$ and $X^+$ respectively.
Figure 21.2. How $X$ and $X^+$ scale singular vectors. Left: $X$ maps the unit right singular vector $v_i$ (blue) to $\delta_i u_i$ (red), stretching it by the singular value $\delta_i = 3$. The unit vector $u_i$ is shown in faint red for reference. Right: $X^+$ maps the unit left singular vector $u_i$ (red) to $(1/\delta_i)v_i$ (blue), compressing it by factor $1/3$. The two operations are exact inverses of each other within the row and column spaces.
Warning · Outside the Subspaces

For a vector $p$ that is not in Row($X$), the product $X^+Xp$ is not equal to $p$. Instead, $X^+Xp = VV^Tp$ is the projection of $p$ onto Row($X$). The pseudo-inverse does not undo the null-space component of $p$ — that information is irretrievably lost when we apply $X$. Similarly, $XX^+q \ne q$ for $q \notin \text{Col}(X)$. The pseudo-inverse is only a true inverse when restricted to the appropriate subspace.

21.5 Pseudo-Inverse and Least-Squares Regression

The most important application of the pseudo-inverse in machine learning is solving the normal equations of linear regression. When $X^TX$ is invertible, Lecture 10's formula $(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$ works. But $X^TX$ is singular whenever $X$ is rank-deficient — a situation that arises routinely when there are more features than training points ($d > n$), when features are collinear, or when the sample points span a proper subspace of feature space. The Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse handles all of these cases gracefully.

21.5.1 The Pseudo-Inverse Solves the Normal Equations

Recall from Lecture 10 that the least-squares problem $\min_w \|Xw - y\|^2$ has solutions characterized by the normal equations $X^TXw = X^Ty$. When $X^TX$ is singular this system has infinitely many solutions. We want to show that $w^+ = X^+y$ is always one of them — for any $X$ and any $y$.

Theorem · Pseudo-Inverse Solves the Normal Equations

For any $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the vector $w^+ = X^+y$ satisfies the normal equations: $$X^TXw^+ = X^Ty.$$

Proof

Substitute $w^+ = X^+y = V\Delta^{-1}U^Ty$ and expand $X^TXw^+$ using compact SVDs. Write $X^T = V\Delta U^T$ and $X = U\Delta V^T$: $$X^TXw^+ = (V\Delta U^T)(U\Delta V^T)(V\Delta^{-1}U^T)y.$$ Group the middle terms: $U^TU = I_r$ cancels the first pair, and $V^TV = I_r$ cancels the second: $$= V\Delta (U^TU) \Delta (V^TV) \Delta^{-1}U^Ty = V\Delta^2\Delta^{-1}U^Ty = V\Delta U^Ty = X^Ty.$$ □

Least-Norm Solution
$$w^+ = X^+y = V\Delta^{-1}U^Ty$$ $$\text{minimizes } \|w\|_2 \text{ subject to } X^TXw = X^Ty$$
Example · Underdetermined Regression

Setup. Consider $n = 2$ training points, $d = 3$ features: $X = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $y = \begin{pmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$.

Normal equations. $X^TX = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$ is singular (rank 2, since col 3 = col 1 + col 2). There are infinitely many solutions to $X^TXw = X^Ty$.

Pseudo-inverse solution. The pseudo-inverse selects the unique solution with smallest $\|w\|_2$. One can verify (by computing the SVD) that $w^+ = X^+y = (1, 3/2, 1/2)^T$ — wait, let's think geometrically: we want the shortest vector $w$ such that $Xw = \hat y$ where $\hat y$ is the projection of $y$ onto Col($X$). Since $X$ has full row rank ($r = 2 = n$) here, $\hat y = y$ and $Xw = y$ is consistent. The minimum-norm solution lies in Row($X$) and is given by $w^+ = X^Ty(XX^T)^{-1} \cdot$... via $X^+$. This is the unique solution with no component in Null($X$) = span$\{(1,1,-1)^T\}/\sqrt{3}$.

Significance. Among all $w$ satisfying $Xw = y$, the pseudo-inverse solution $w^+ = X^+y$ is the sparsest in energy. It avoids arbitrary large weights that would arise from any particular choice of basis for the solution space.

21.5.2 Least-Norm Solution and Ridge Regression

The pseudo-inverse gives a theoretically elegant solution, but it has a practical weakness: if any singular value $\delta_i$ is very small, its reciprocal $1/\delta_i$ becomes very large, causing $X^+y$ to be dominated by that direction. A singular value of $0.001$ becomes $1000$ in $\Delta^{-1}$, potentially swamping all other directions and producing an unstable, high-variance solution.

Definition · Ridge Regression (Tikhonov Regularization)

The ridge regression estimator with regularization parameter $\lambda > 0$ is $$\hat{w}_\lambda = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{w} \left[\|Xw - y\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|^2\right] = (X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty.$$ In terms of the SVD, writing $X = U\Delta V^T$: $$\hat{w}_\lambda = V \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\delta_1}{\delta_1^2+\lambda}, \ldots, \frac{\delta_r}{\delta_r^2+\lambda}\right) U^Ty.$$

Compare the effective weight that each singular direction receives. The pseudo-inverse weights direction $i$ by $1/\delta_i$, which blows up as $\delta_i \to 0$. Ridge weights direction $i$ by $\delta_i/(\delta_i^2+\lambda)$, which peaks at $1/(2\sqrt{\lambda})$ and then smoothly returns to zero as $\delta_i \to 0$. Ridge regression does not abruptly threshold any singular value — it gradually down-weights all directions, with the most aggressive shrinkage in the directions corresponding to the smallest singular values.

Figure 21.5. Effect of small singular values on coefficient magnitude. Left: Effective weight on each singular direction as a function of $\delta$. The pseudo-inverse (red dashed) diverges as $\delta \to 0$. Ridge regression with $\lambda = 0.01$ (blue), $\lambda = 0.1$ (green), and $\lambda = 1.0$ (gold) all remain bounded. Right: For an example spectrum with singular values $\{4.0, 2.5, 0.8, 0.05, 0.005\}$, the pseudo-inverse coefficient for the fifth direction blows up (truncated at 80 for display), while ridge regression with $\lambda = 0.1$ or $\lambda = 1.0$ keeps all coefficients manageable. Ridge regression provides a continuous analog to discarding small singular values.
Intuition · Truncated SVD vs. Ridge

There are two strategies for handling small singular values. Truncated SVD sets a hard threshold $\tau$: any singular value below $\tau$ is treated as zero and dropped. This is a binary decision — the direction is either fully included or fully excluded. Ridge regression instead applies a soft threshold: every direction is retained but down-weighted by a factor $\delta_i^2/(\delta_i^2 + \lambda)$. Directions with large $\delta_i$ are barely shrunk; directions with small $\delta_i$ are shrunk heavily. The result is a smooth interpolation that avoids the instability of hard cutoffs while still suppressing noisy low-variance directions.

ⓘ
Connection to Chapter 4 (GDA): The ridge regression solution can be interpreted as the posterior mean in a Bayesian linear regression model with a spherical Gaussian prior $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, (1/\lambda)I)$. This prior encodes the belief that weights should be small, exactly analogous to how GDA's Gaussian assumption provides regularization for classification.

21.6 Improving Neural Network Generalization

Neural networks can approximate virtually any function, which is both their greatest strength and their greatest weakness: given enough capacity, a network will memorize the training set perfectly and generalize poorly to new data. We say the network overfits when its training loss is far lower than its test loss. The classical tools for fighting overfitting — regularization, data augmentation, ensemble methods — all apply to neural networks, though they manifest in forms tailored to the deep learning setting.

We survey seven techniques, focusing on the two most theoretically interesting: data augmentation and L2 regularization (weight decay). The connection between them and the SVD machinery of this chapter is not superficial — both can be understood as injecting prior knowledge into the learning algorithm to compensate for limited data.

21.6.1 Data Augmentation

When collecting more data is not possible, the next best thing is to generate more training examples by transforming the existing ones in ways that preserve the label. For image classification, this is especially natural: a cat photographed upside-down is still a cat. By augmenting the training set with flipped, rotated, cropped, brightness-adjusted, and noise-corrupted versions of each image, we effectively multiply the dataset size and force the network to learn features that are invariant to the applied transformations.

Definition · Data Augmentation

Given a training set $\{(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^n$, data augmentation replaces or supplements each example $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ with a collection of transformed copies $\{(T_k(x^{(i)}), y^{(i)})\}_{k=1}^K$, where each transformation $T_k: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{X}$ is chosen such that $T_k(x^{(i)})$ has the same label $y^{(i)}$. Common transformations for image data include horizontal/vertical flips, random crops, rotation by a small angle $\theta$, additive Gaussian noise $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$, brightness and contrast adjustment, and color jitter.

Figure 21.6. Eight variants of a synthetic image under common data augmentation transformations. Top row (left to right): original, horizontal flip, random crop and rescale, rotation by 15°. Bottom row: brightness increase (+30%), contrast stretching, additive Gaussian noise ($\sigma = 0.08$), and color jitter. All eight variants carry the same class label as the original. Training a CNN on all variants instead of just the original forces the network to develop translation-, rotation-, and illumination-invariant features.

Advanced augmentation strategies go beyond simple geometric transforms. Cutout randomly masks a rectangular patch of the image, forcing the network to classify from partial information. Mixup creates convex combinations of pairs of images and their labels: $\tilde{x} = \lambda x_i + (1-\lambda) x_j$, $\tilde{y} = \lambda y_i + (1-\lambda) y_j$. CutMix pastes a patch from one image into another. Research by Hendrycks and colleagues found that such augmentation can match the benefit of a 10$\times$ increase in model size for in-distribution accuracy, and the equivalent of 1000$\times$ more labeled data for out-of-distribution robustness — remarkable leverage from transformations that cost nearly nothing to compute.

Warning · Label-Preserving Augmentation

Every augmentation must preserve the label. Geometric transforms like flips and rotations are always safe for natural image classes. But augmentations that mix examples from different classes (Mixup, CutMix) create examples with soft labels: if image $x_i$ is a bird and $x_j$ is a turtle and $\lambda = 0.5$, the mixed example should be labeled $(0.5, 0.5)$ across the two classes, not hard-labeled as either. Using hard labels for mixed examples leads to inconsistent training signals. Always verify that the augmented examples and their labels are logically consistent for your domain.

21.6.2 L2 Regularization and Weight Decay

L2 regularization adds a penalty on the squared magnitude of the weights to the training objective. In neural networks the same technique is sometimes called weight decay, because its effect during gradient descent is to multiply each weight by a factor slightly less than one at every step, causing weights to decay toward zero unless reinforced by the gradient signal.

Definition · L2 Regularization for Neural Networks

Given a cost function $J(w)$ (sum of per-example losses), the L2-regularized objective is $$J_\lambda(w) = J(w) + \lambda \|w\|^2$$ where $w \in \mathbb{R}^P$ is the vector of all network weights (possibly including biases) and $\lambda > 0$ is the regularization hyperparameter. The gradient becomes $$\nabla_w J_\lambda = \nabla_w J + 2\lambda w.$$ The SGD update for weight $w_i$ is therefore $$\Delta w_i = -\varepsilon \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_i} - 2\varepsilon\lambda w_i = -\varepsilon \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_i} + \underbrace{(1 - 2\varepsilon\lambda)w_i - w_i}_{\text{decay term}},$$ so at each step every weight is multiplied by the decay factor $(1 - 2\varepsilon\lambda) < 1$ before the gradient step.

The name "weight decay" is apt: if learning stopped, every weight would decay geometrically toward zero at rate $(1 - 2\varepsilon\lambda)$ per step. In practice, the gradient term continuously reinforces weights that are useful for prediction, so they settle at nonzero values determined by the balance between the learning signal and the decay pressure. Weights that are not reinforced by the data do decay toward zero, effectively performing automatic feature selection.

Figure 21.7. Effect of L2 regularization on a neural network decision boundary for a two-class classification problem in 2D weight space. Left: Without regularization ($\lambda = 0$), the network overfits — the decision boundary (solid black) follows the training data closely but deviates from the Bayes-optimal boundary (dashed purple). Right: With $\lambda = 0.2$, the regularized boundary (solid black) is smoother and closer to the Bayes-optimal curve. Blue points: class 0; red points: class 1. Background shading shows the posterior class probability. Regularization effectively biases the model toward simpler, smoother boundaries.
Theorem · Weight Decay Equivalent to Ridge Regression

For a single-layer linear neural network $\hat{y} = Xw$ with squared loss, L2 regularization with parameter $\lambda$ produces exactly the ridge regression solution: $$w^* = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_w \left[\|Xw - y\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|^2\right] = (X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty = \hat{w}_\lambda.$$ The SVD interpretation from Section 21.5 applies: each singular direction is shrunk by the factor $\delta_i^2/(\delta_i^2 + \lambda)$, with the most aggressive shrinkage in low-variance directions.

Data Science Application · AlexNet and Practical Training

AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), the network that launched modern deep learning by winning ImageNet with a 10% margin, trained with both L2 regularization and momentum. The combined update rule was: compute the gradient of the loss plus regularization term, then apply the momentum algorithm. Concretely, at each step a velocity vector $v$ was updated as $v \leftarrow \mu v - \varepsilon(\nabla_w J + 2\lambda w)$, and then weights updated as $w \leftarrow w + v$. With $\lambda = 0.0005$, the weight decay factor per step was approximately $0.999$, providing gentle but persistent regularization throughout training. This combination — momentum for faster convergence, L2 regularization for better generalization — remains a baseline in deep learning practice today.

TechniqueMechanismWhen to Use
More dataReduces estimation variance directlyAlways, when available
Data augmentationExpands effective dataset; enforces invariancesImages, audio, sequences
Feature selectionRemoves uninformative inputsHigh-dimensional tabular data
L2 regularizationPenalizes large weights; smooths boundaryAlmost universally
Early stoppingStops before overfitting; implicit regularizationAlways monitor val. loss
DropoutRandomly disables units; ensemble effectFully connected layers
Ensemble methodsAverages multiple modelsWhen compute allows

✦ Chapter Summary

This chapter developed two interconnected themes. The first is the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse, which the compact SVD defines beautifully: $X^+ = V\Delta^{-1}U^T$. We proved that $XX^+$ and $X^+X$ are orthogonal projectors onto the column and row spaces of $X$, that the pseudo-inverse reduces to the ordinary inverse when one exists, and that $w^+ = X^+y$ always solves the normal equations. We also saw that small singular values destabilize $X^+$ and that ridge regression provides a principled smooth remedy. The second theme was neural network generalization: data augmentation expands the effective training set by applying label-preserving transformations, while L2 regularization penalizes large weights and, in the linear case, reduces exactly to ridge regression — closing the loop between the SVD theory of the first half and the deep learning practice of the second.

COMPACT SVD

$X = U\Delta V^T$ with $U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$, $\Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}$ invertible diagonal, $V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, all with orthonormal columns. Rank $r$ equals the number of positive singular values. The compact SVD discards zero singular values, making $\Delta$ invertible.

MOORE-PENROSE PSEUDO-INVERSE

$X^+ = V\Delta^{-1}U^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$. Defined for any matrix. Reduces to $X^{-1}$ when $X$ is invertible. Zero singular values are not inverted. The pseudo-inverse is the unique matrix satisfying the four Penrose conditions.

PRODUCTS $XX^+$ AND $X^+X$

$XX^+ = UU^T$ is the orthogonal projector onto Col($X$); $X^+X = VV^T$ is the projector onto Row($X$). Both are symmetric and idempotent. When $r = n$, $XX^+ = I_n$; when $r = d$, $X^+X = I_d$.

SINGULAR VALUE INVERSION

$X^T$ and $X$ share the same singular values $\delta_i$; $X^+$ replaces each $\delta_i$ with $1/\delta_i$. The singular vectors are the same: $X^+$ and $X^T$ span identical subspaces but scale differently. $(X^+)^T = U\Delta^{-1}V^T$.

FOUR FUNDAMENTAL SUBSPACES

The subspaces of $X^+$ are exactly those of $X$ with row space and column space swapped: Col($X^+$) = Row($X$), Row($X^+$) = Col($X$), Null($X^+$) = Null($X^T$). Equivalently, $X^+$ has the same four subspaces as $X^T$.

ROW-COLUMN BIJECTION

$X$ restricted to Row($X$) is a bijection onto Col($X$); $X^+$ restricted to Col($X$) is its inverse. Right singular vectors $v_i$ map to $\delta_i u_i$ under $X$; left singular vectors $u_i$ map to $(1/\delta_i)v_i$ under $X^+$. Vectors outside these subspaces are projected before mapping.

LEAST-NORM SOLUTION

$w^+ = X^+y$ always satisfies the normal equations $X^TXw = X^Ty$. When the normal equations have multiple solutions, $w^+$ is the unique solution of minimum Euclidean norm — it has no component in Null($X$). This is the correct pseudo-inverse for least-squares regression in all cases.

RIDGE REGRESSION

$(X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty$ shrinks each singular direction by $\delta_i^2/(\delta_i^2+\lambda)$. Prevents blow-up from small singular values. As $\lambda \to 0$ it approaches $X^+y$; as $\lambda \to \infty$ it approaches $0$. Equivalent to L2 regularization in linear networks.

DATA AUGMENTATION

Applies label-preserving transformations (flip, crop, rotate, noise) to training examples to increase effective dataset size and enforce invariances. Can match the benefit of 10$\times$ more model parameters or 1000$\times$ more labeled data for robustness. Mixed-example methods (Mixup, CutMix) require soft labels.

WEIGHT DECAY / L2 REGULARIZATION

Adds $\lambda\|w\|^2$ to the loss; gradient descent update becomes $w_i \leftarrow (1 - 2\varepsilon\lambda)w_i - \varepsilon\partial J/\partial w_i$. The factor $(1-2\varepsilon\lambda)$ decays weights toward zero at each step. Prevents overfitting by keeping weights small; used in AlexNet with $\lambda = 0.0005$.

Exercises

Exercise 21.1  ·  PSEUDO-INVERSE COMPUTATION
Computing and Verifying the Moore-Penrose Pseudo-Inverse

Let $X = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$.

  1. Find the compact SVD of $X$ by inspection. What is the rank $r$? Write down $U$, $\Delta$, and $V$ explicitly.
  2. Compute $X^+ = V\Delta^{-1}U^T$. Verify that $XX^+ = UU^T$ and $X^+X = VV^T$ by direct matrix multiplication.
  3. Is $X^+$ a right inverse, a left inverse, both, or neither? Justify by checking whether $XX^+ = I$ and/or $X^+X = I$.
  4. In a regression task, $y = (4, 6)^T$. Compute $w^+ = X^+y$. Show that $w^+$ lies in Row($X$) (i.e., Null($X$)$\perp$). What is the null space of $X$, and why does $w^+$ have no component in it?
Exercise 21.2  ·  PROJECTORS AND SUBSPACES
Verifying Projector Properties in a Document Retrieval Application

In information retrieval, a term-document matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ has $n$ terms and $d$ documents. Suppose $X$ has rank $r < \min(n, d)$.

  1. Prove from first principles (using the compact SVD) that $(XX^+)^2 = XX^+$ and $(XX^+)^T = XX^+$. Conclude that $XX^+$ is an orthogonal projector.
  2. A query vector $q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ represents a search query. Interpret $X^+(X^+)^T q$ geometrically. What subspace does it project onto?
  3. Show that for any $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the vector $XX^+y$ is the closest point to $y$ in Col($X$) — i.e., that $\|y - XX^+y\| \le \|y - Xw\|$ for all $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$. (Hint: use the fact that $I - XX^+$ projects onto Null($X^T$), which is orthogonal to Col($X$).)
  4. Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) computes $X^+$ to find a low-rank approximation of the query-document similarity. Explain why using only the top-$k$ singular values (truncated SVD) rather than all $r$ is beneficial for retrieval, in terms of the noise model for term-document matrices.
Exercise 21.3  ·  NORMAL EQUATIONS AND LEAST NORM
Underdetermined Linear Regression in Genomics

In genomics, a typical regression problem has $n = 500$ patients and $d = 20{,}000$ gene expression features — far more features than samples.

  1. Prove that when $n < d$, the matrix $X^TX \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ is always singular. (Hint: consider the rank of $X^TX$ using the rank inequality $\text{rank}(AB) \le \min(\text{rank}(A), \text{rank}(B))$.)
  2. Let $\mathcal{S} = \{w : X^TXw = X^Ty\}$ be the solution set of the normal equations. Prove that $w^+ = X^+y$ minimizes $\|w\|_2$ over $\mathcal{S}$. (Hint: write any solution as $w = w^+ + z$ where $z \in \text{Null}(X)$, and show $\|w^+ + z\|^2 \ge \|w^+\|^2$ using orthogonality.)
  3. Compute $w^+$ for the simple case $X = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $y = (2)$. List all solutions to $X^TXw = X^Ty$ and verify $w^+$ has the smallest norm.
  4. In the genomics setting, explain why the minimum-norm solution may not be the most scientifically useful, and propose an alternative regularization strategy (e.g., $\ell_1$ regularization / LASSO) that would yield a sparse solution and its practical advantages for gene discovery.
Exercise 21.4  ·  RIDGE REGRESSION AND SINGULAR VALUES
Regularization Path and Shrinkage in Medical Imaging

Consider fitting a linear model to $n = 100$ MRI scans with $d = 500$ features, where the design matrix has singular values $\delta_1 = 8, \delta_2 = 4, \delta_3 = 0.5, \delta_4 = 0.01$.

  1. Derive the SVD formula for the ridge regression solution $\hat{w}_\lambda = V\operatorname{diag}(\delta_i/(\delta_i^2+\lambda))U^Ty$ by completing the following: take the gradient of $\|Xw-y\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|^2$, set it to zero, and simplify using the SVD of $X^TX = V\Delta^2V^T$.
  2. For each of $\delta_1, \delta_2, \delta_3, \delta_4$, compute the shrinkage factor $\delta_i^2/(\delta_i^2 + \lambda)$ for $\lambda \in \{0.001, 0.1, 1.0, 10\}$. Present as a table and describe the pattern: which singular directions are most strongly shrunk?
  3. Plot (by hand or describe) the "regularization path" — how the contribution of each singular direction to $\hat{w}_\lambda$ changes as $\lambda$ increases from $0$ to $\infty$. At what value of $\lambda$ does direction 4 lose essentially all influence?
  4. In a clinical application, discuss the trade-off between using the pseudo-inverse ($\lambda = 0$) and ridge regression ($\lambda > 0$) when the goal is to identify which brain regions are most predictive of a disease outcome. What are the risks of each approach?
Exercise 21.5  ·  DATA AUGMENTATION AND WEIGHT DECAY
Generalization Strategies for a Small-Data Medical Image Classifier

You are training a CNN to classify skin lesions as benign or malignant from dermoscopy images. Your training set has only $n = 800$ labeled images.

  1. List five specific data augmentation transforms you would apply to dermoscopy images and justify why each is label-preserving. Are there any transforms you would not apply, and why?
  2. Suppose you apply horizontal flips, 4 rotation angles, and 2 brightness levels to each image. How many effective training examples does this create? If the baseline test accuracy is 72% and each doubling of the dataset improves accuracy by approximately 3%, what test accuracy do you expect?
  3. Derive the weight decay update rule: starting from $\Delta w_i = -\varepsilon \partial J_\lambda / \partial w_i$, expand to show explicitly the decay factor $(1 - 2\varepsilon\lambda)$. If $\varepsilon = 0.01$ and $\lambda = 0.001$, what is the decay factor per step, and how many steps until a weight that receives no gradient signal decays to half its original value?
  4. An experiment finds that applying L2 regularization with $\lambda = 0.01$ improves validation accuracy from 74% to 79%. However, a colleague suggests that simply training for fewer epochs (early stopping) would have the same effect without adding a hyperparameter. Design an experiment to test this claim, specifying what quantities you would measure and how you would decide which method is superior.
